newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian budget hit as weak, ineffective.
newsitem.headline: Australian budget hit as weak, ineffective.

text.p: Australia's modest 1997/98 budget drew criticism on Wednesday from commentators and financial analysts who accused the conservative government of going soft on spending cuts and deserting the unemployed.

But Prime Minister John Howard and Treasurer Peter Costello, in a round of media interviews, defended their mid-term budget as fair but tough, pointing to government belt-tightening and an improved bottom line.
"That's not treading water, it is swimming freestyle dramatically," Howard said in a radio interview.

The budget for the year from July projected an underlying deficit of A$3.9 billion (US$3.0 billion), down from A$6.9 billion and rising to a A$1.6 billion surplus in 1998/99, the first in almost a decade.

The improved performance was achieved by modest cuts and a strengthening economy, without the massive cuts in the first budget which sparked violent street protests, flag-burnings and a storming of parliament house last year.
But newspapers hit the government for wasting the opportunity to make significant economic reforms, accusing it of going soft in preparation for re-election.
"Its weakness is in the political thrust, directed at the next election," said the national daily, The Australian.
"Mr Costello has set the scene for electoral vote-buying which would threaten the government's economic management achievements," the newspaper said.
The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper said in its editorial: "...the Prime Minister Mr Howard and Mr Costello have given in to the temptation to put the fiscal axe back in the shed...".
The budget also failed to tackle high unemployment, projecting only a minimal fall in the number of jobless from around 8.75 percent, said critics.
"What we need are some proactive strategies that are going to target, particularly the long-term unemployed and disadvantaged regions," said welfare worker Peter Walsh.
Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said the budget, with no major shocks and a tax break for savers, would help the Liberal-National coalition revive its sagging popularity.
The government's support halfway through its first three-year term is the lowest since its election as voters desert it for populist, right-winger Pauline Hanson's new One Nation Party.
